name: Nassau Hall
description: The oldest building at [[Princeton University]] and the largest in New Jersey when it was built in 1756. It served as the home of the American government from July to October 1783.

name: Morven
description: Built in 1754 by [[Richard Stockton (1730-1781)]], a signer of the [[United States Declaration of Independence|Declaration of Independence]]. It served as the New Jersey Governors mansion from 1945 until 1982 and is now a museum.

name: Maclean House
description: [[John Witherspoon]] lived in this home for the president of the College of New Jersey (later [[Princeton University]]) between 1768 and 1779. During this time he also served as a delegate to the [[Continental Congress]] and signed the [[United States Declaration of Independence|Declaration of Independence]].

name: Joseph Henry House
description: Home of [[Joseph Henry]], whose scientific research on electromagnetic self-[[inductance]] led to the [[electrical telegraph]]. He was also the first Secretary of the [[Smithsonian Institution]].

name: Prospect
description: A fine example of [[John Notman]]'s architecture. It formerly served as the official home of the president of Princeton University, and is now the faculty club. [[Woodrow Wilson]] lived here from 1902 to 1910, prior to entering politics.

name: Westland Mansion
image: 15 Hodge Road, Princeton, NJ - Grover Cleveland home.jpg
description: Mid-19th-century mansion built by [[Robert F. Stockton]] and later home of [[Grover Cleveland]] after he left the [[White House]].

name: Albert Einstein House
description: The home of [[Albert Einstein]] after his flight from Germany in 1933 until his death in 1955.

name: University Cottage Club
description: One of Princeton's historic [[Eating clubs at Princeton University|eating clubs]], designed by [[McKim, Mead & White]]

name: The Barracks
description: Built late 17th century, considered to be the oldest house still standing in Princeton.  Built by the grandfather of [[Richard Stockton (Continental Congressman)|Richard Stockton]], a signer of the [[United States Declaration of Independence|Declaration of Independence]].  The name derives from its presumed use as a barracks in the [[French and Indian War]] or [[w:American Revolution|American Revolution]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hageman|first1=John Frelinghuysen|title=History of Princeton and Its Institutions, Volume 1|date=1878|publisher=J.B. Lippincott & Company|location=Philadelphia|page=[https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog/page/n90 65]|url=https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog|quote=barracks.}}</ref>

name: Princeton Cemetery
image: Presidents row, old Princeton burying ground-LCCN2008679656.jpg
description: Burial place of many prominent figures including [[Jonathan Edwards (theologian)|Jonathan Edwards]], [[Aaron Burr]], [[Grover Cleveland]], [[Paul Tulane]], and [[Kurt Gödel]] among many others.

name: Bainbridge House
description: Built by Job Stockton of brickwork with wooden keystone lintels to a central hall plan, it retains much of its original woodwork and corner fireplaces.  It was the birthplace of Commodore [[William Bainbridge]] and served as the headquarters of the British in 1776 before the [[Battle of Princeton]].  It has long served as the museum of the Princeton Historical Society.

name: Peacock Inn
description: 18th-century home of [[Provincial Congress of New Jersey|Jonathan Deare]], moved to Bayard Lane in 1875 by [[William Libbey]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hageman|first1=John Frelinghuysen|title=History of Princeton and Its Institutions, Volume 1|date=1879|publisher=J.B. Lippincott & Company|page=[https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog/page/n125 96]|url=https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog|quote=Jonathan deare University Hotel.}}</ref>  Since 1911 an inn and restaurant, one of the finest in the state.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Levin|first1=Eric|title=The 25 Best Restaurants of 2014|url=http://njmonthly.com/articles/eat-drink/25-best-restaurants-nj-2014/|website=New Jersey Monthly|date=July 15, 2014}}</ref>

name: Beatty House
image: GENERAL VIEW OF EXTERIOR - Colonel Jacob Hyer House, 19 Vandeventer Street, Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,10-1.tif
description: Built by Jacob Hyer, by whose name it is sometimes known, the house was purchased by Erkuries Beatty in 1816.  The [[Marquis de Lafayette]] is known to have stayed here July 15, 1825.  It was originally located on Nassau Street opposite Bainbridge House and was moved to its current location by James Vandeventer in 1875.<ref>{{cite web|title=Princeton's Historic Sites and People|url=http://www.princetonhistory.org/collections/historic-sites.cfm|website=Historical Society of Princeton}}</ref>

name: Stanhope Hall
description: The third building of Princeton University's campus, designed by [[Benjamin Henry Latrobe]] and originally home to the library, study halls, and literary societies.  Later known as Geological Hall, in 1915 it was named in honor of [[Samuel Stanhope Smith]], president of the university at the time of its construction.

name: Nassau Club
description: [[Gentlemen's Club]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] founded in 1889 by [[Woodrow Wilson]].  The clubhouse was originally built in 1813-14 as the home of [[Samuel Miller (theologian)|Samuel Miller]], the second professor of the [[Princeton Theological Seminary]], on land belonging to his father-in-law, [[Second Continental Congress|Continental Congressman]] [[Jonathan Dickinson Sergeant]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hageman|first1=John Frelinghuysen|title=History of Princeton and Its Institutions, Volume 1|date=1878|publisher=J.B. Lippincott & Company|location=Philadelphia|page=[https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog/page/n152 123]|url=https://archive.org/details/historyprinceto00hagegoog|quote=Samuel Miller home.}}</ref>

name: Alexander Hall (Princeton Theological Seminary)
description: The original building of the [[Princeton Theological Seminary]], patterned after [[Nassau Hall]], and designed by [[John McComb Jr.]]

name: Palmer House
image: EDGAR PALMER HOUSE, PRINCETON, MERCER COUNTY, NJ.jpg
description: Built by [[Charles Steadman]] for [[Robert F. Stockton]].  It is one of Steadman's earlier works and is noted for its elegant and restrained design.  The building now serves as the guest house of Princeton University.

name: 12 Morven Place
description: Early Charles Steadman house with a center portico of [[Ionic order|Ionic]] columns.

name: 20 Alexander Street
image: VIEW OF FRONT FACADE - 20 Alexander Street (House), Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,15-1.tif
description: Designed by Charles Steadman as part of Princeton's first housing development, with the houses marked by [[unity in variety]].

name: Miller Chapel
description: The chapel of the [[Princeton Theological Seminary]], designed by Charles Steadman in [[stucco]]ed brick with a simple [[Doric Order|Doric]] portico.

name: John Breckenridge House
image: GENERAL VIEW OF FRONT FACADE - Professor John Breckenridge House, 72 Library Place, Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,23-1.tif
description: Built by Charles Steadman the exterior details are especially fine and the facade well balanced.  Named after longtime owner Professor John Breckenridge, uncle of [[John C. Breckinridge]].  It is thought to have originally had a small center porch, since replaced by stairs. [[Woodrow Wilson]] bought this house in 1889 and it is sometimes known by his name.

name: Nassau Presbyterian Church
image: GENERAL VIEW OF FRONT FACADE - First Presbyterian Church, 61 Nassau Street, Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,25-1.tif
description: Built by Charles Steadman in [[Greek Revival architecture|Greek Revival]] style using stuccoed brick, and is a fine example of his use of the monumental, with a recessed porch flanked by [[pilasters]].

name: 40-42 Mercer Street
description: A double house indicating that Charles Steadman had begun to build houses for the working class.

name: Walter Lowrie House
description: [[Official residence]] of the president of [[Princeton University]].  Built by [[Robert F. Stockton]] for his son [[John P. Stockton]], designed by [[John Notman]].  Later home to [[Paul Tulane]], founder of [[Tulane University]].  From 1930-1959, it was home to [[Kierkegaard]]ian scholar [[Walter Lowrie (author)|Walter Lowrie]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Leitch|first1=Alexander|title=A Princeton Companion|date=1978|publisher=Princeton University Press|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/CampusWWW/Companion/lowrie_house.html}}</ref>

name: Ivy Hall
description: A small gothic building designed by John Notman as the home of the short-lived Princeton University law school.  It gave its name to [[Ivy Club]], the university's first [[Eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] which was housed there from its founding in 1879 to 1883.  Now the property of [[Trinity Church, Princeton|Trinity Church]] and home to its choir.

name: Springdale
description: Designed by John Notman in 1851 for Richard Stockton, son of [[Commodore (rank)|Commodore]] [[Robert F. Stockton]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Springdale|url=http://princeton.pastperfect-online.com/37602cgi/mweb.exe?request=record&id=000750B3-5705-4F40-85DF-546822594903&type=102|website=Historical Society of Princeton}}</ref>  Now the [[official residence]] of the president of [[Princeton Theological Seminary]].

name: Guernsey Hall
image: VIEW OF STAIRHALL - Princeton University, Guernsey Hall, 63 Lovers Lane, Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,20-9.tif
description: Designed by John Notman for the Stockton family.  It is similar in design to [[Prospect House (Princeton, New Jersey)|Prospect House]].  It is noted for its central rotunda with a spiraling staircase with a circular skylight framed by octagonal panels.

name: Marquand Park
description: The park was laid out by John Notman as a romantic landscape with many exotic plants and trees.  It is named after former owner [[Allan Marquand]] whose descendants turned the property into a public park.

name: Nassau Christian Center
description: Built as Second Presbyterian Church of Princeton, the church was originally planned to have an exceedingly tall spire which was not added for cost reasons.  It is now home to an [[Assemblies of God]] congregation.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hageman|first1=John Frelinghuysen|title=History of Princeton and Its Institutions, Volume 2|date=1879|publisher=J.B. Lippincott & Company|pages=200–208|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XzwVAAAAYAAJ&q=%22Second+Presbyterian+Church%22+Princeton&pg=PA201}}</ref>

name: Chancellor Green Library
image: AmCyc Princeton - Library of the College of New Jersey.jpg
description: A [[Venetian Gothic architecture|Venetian Gothic]] structure designed by [[William Appleton Potter]] as the first standalone library of Princeton University.  It is noted for its multi-colored tile roof, detailed stone work, stained glass windows, and striking interior.

name: Trinity Episcopal Church
description: An historic [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopalian]] congregation.  The original 1833 [[Greek Revival architecture|Greek Revival]] building by [[Charles Steadman]] was replaced in 1870 by this [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] design by [[Richard Upjohn]].  A major reconstruction was undertaken by [[Ralph Adams Cram]] in 1914.

name: Stuart Hall
description: The main classroom building of the Princeton Theological Seminary, designed by William Appleton Potter in Venetian Gothic style.

name: Murray-Dodge Hall
description: Built for the Princeton University [[Evangelical]] Philadelphian Society in 1879 (Murray Hall) and 1900 (Dodge Hall) by [[Richard Morris Hunt]].  Murray Hall, known as Theater Intime, is now a theater and Dodge Hall, commonly called Murray-Dodge, is home to the Office of Religious Life.

name: 32 Wiggins Street
description: A fine example of "carpenters" [[Queen Anne style architecture in the United States|Queen Anne]] architecture with lapped shingles and a hexagonal tower.  It is typical of the spacious [[Victorian house|Victorian]] houses in the neighborhood.

name: William Berryman Scott House
description: Designed by [[A. Page Brown]] for [[William Berryman Scott]], it is an interesting example of [[Shingle style architecture]] with ample proportions and skillful use of material.<ref>{{cite news|title=Two Houses are in Focus|url=http://papersofprinceton.princeton.edu/princetonperiodicals/cgi-bin/princetonperiodicals?a=d&d=TownTopics19781004-01.2.32&srpos=5&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-%2256+Bayard%22------#|newspaper=Town Topics|date=October 4, 1978}}</ref>

name: Alexander Hall (Princeton University
image: Alexander Hall at Princeton University, NJ.jpg
description: A [[Richardsonian Romanesque]] concert hall designed by William Appleton Potter.  The massive stone walls are punctuated by arches, with turrets at the four corners.

name: Tiger Inn
description: Third [[Eating club (Princeton University)|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]], with reputation as the [[Animal House]] of Princeton.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rojas|first1=Cristina|title=Leaders of Tiger Inn, a Princeton eating club, resign after party|url=http://www.nj.com/mercer/index.ssf/2014/03/leaders_of_tiger_inn_a_princeton_eating_club_resign_after_party.html|website=Times of Trenton}}</ref>

name: Blair Tower
image: Stronghold Princeton University New Jersey USA Jazz-Face Mod.jpg
description: One of the early Collegiate Gothic buildings at Princeton University, designed by [[Cope and Stewardson]] to provide a monumental staircase and arch entrance from the [[Princeton (NJT station)|Princeton train station (1865)]].

name: Lower Pyne
description: Designed by [[Raleigh C. Gildersleeve]] for [[Moses Taylor Pyne]] in [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor Revival]] style.  It originally housed dormitories above commercial space as a way to integrate the Princeton University campus with the town.

name: Old Princeton Bank and Trust
image: GENERAL VIEW OF FRONT FACADE - Princeton Bank and Trust, 12-14 Nassau Street, Princeton, Mercer County, NJ HABS NJ,11-PRINT,13-2.tif
description: Designed by William E. Stone in [[Dutch Colonial Revival architecture|Dutch Colonial]] style, the building demonstrates diversity of architectural styles within the architectural unity of the town.

name: Ivy Club
description: Oldest and most prestigious [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]], first housed in [[Princeton Law School|Ivy Hall]], from which it got its name.<ref>{{cite news |title=At Ivy Club, A Trip Back to Elitism |first=Monique |last=Yazigi |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/16/style/at-ivy-club-a-trip-back-to-elitism.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=May 16, 1999 |access-date=February 2, 2011}}</ref>

name: Thanet Lodge
description: The 1902 mansion of famed archaeologist and Olympic athlete [[William Libbey]], now home to the [[Lewis School of Princeton]]

name: FitzRandolph Gate
description: The main gate of Princeton University, designed by [[McKim, Mead & White]] using adapted [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] [[Wrought iron|ironwork]].  It is named after Nathaniel FitzRandolph, who donated the land on which Nassau Hall sits.

name: Colonial Club
description: Fifth oldest [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]], referred to as "flamboyant Colonial" by [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]] in [[This Side of Paradise]]

name: Cap and Gown Club
description: The only [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]] to stay at the same location since its founding.  The current clubhouse is the third on site.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cap & Gown Club|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/Campus/text_Cap.html|website=Princeton University}}</ref>  Members perpetrated the [[Princeton Branch#The Great Dinky Robbery|Great Dinky Robbery]] of 1963.

name: Campus Club
description: Former [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]] closed in 2005 and turned into a student lounge

name: Palmer Physical Laboratory
description: The former Palmer Physical Laboratory, built 1910 to house the Princeton University Physics Department, home to lectures by Albert Einstein and work on the [[Manhattan Project]], renovated and expanded in 2000 into the Frist Campus Center<ref>{{cite web|title=Campus Center Iconography|url=https://www.princeton.edu/frist/iconography/i5.shtml|website=Frist Campus Center|publisher=Princeton University}}</ref>

name: Cannon Club
description: One of the [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating clubs]] at [[Princeton University]], closed in the early 1970s following racially charged incidents, reopened 2011

name: Princeton United Methodist Church
description: Founded in 1847, the present sanctuary was dedicated in 1911 on property donated by [[Moses Taylor Pyne]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Church History|url=http://princetonumc.org/about_us/church-history/|website=Princeton United Methodist Church}}</ref>

name: Princeton University Press
description: Founded by Whitney Darrow, with the financial support of [[Charles Scribner II|Charles Scribner]], as a [[printing press]] to serve the Princeton community in 1905, with a distinctive building designed by [[Ernest Flagg]]<ref>{{cite book|last1=Letich|first1=Alexander|title=A Princeton Companion|date=1978|publisher=Princeton University Press|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/CampusWWW/Companion/princeton_university_press.html|access-date=2015-07-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171019002811/http://etcweb.princeton.edu/CampusWWW/Companion/princeton_university_press.html|archive-date=2017-10-19|url-status=dead}}</ref>

name: Graduate College
image: Princeton University Graduate College, NJ - looking north.jpg
description: Designed by [[Ralph Adams Cram]] and contains some of the most spectacular Collegiate Gothic architecture on Princeton's campus, including [[Cleveland Tower]], Proctor Hall, and the Van Dyke Library.

name: Charter Club
description: Ninth [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] at [[Princeton University]], party in 1988 sent 45 to the hospital<ref>{{cite news|last1=Bloom|first1=Craig|title=Clubs at Princeton Curb Drinking|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/02/12/nyregion/clubs-at-princeton-curb-drinking.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=February 12, 1989}}</ref>

name: University Dining Halls
description: Designed by [[Frank Miles Day|Day]] and [[Charles Klauder|Klauder]], a complex of five Gothic dining halls arranged around a central kitchen.  The structure is named Madison Hall after alumnus [[James Madison]].  At present only two of the halls are used for dining.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Leitch|first1=Alexander|title=Madison Hall|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/CampusWWW/Companion/madison_hall.html|website=Princeton University}}</ref>

name: Quadrangle Club
description: One of the [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating clubs]] at [[Princeton University]], described by [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]] in ''[[This Side of Paradise]]'' as "Literary Quadrangle"<ref>Tumball, Andrew.  ''Scott Fitzgerald''.  New York: Grove Press, 2001: p. 57</ref>

name: Tower Club
description: One of the [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating clubs]] at [[Princeton University]], formed 1902

name: Terrace Club
description: One of the [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating clubs]] at [[Princeton University]].  The clubhouse was reconstructed on the former home of [[John Grier Hibben]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Terrace Club|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/Campus/text_Terrace.html|website=Princeton University}}</ref>

name: Princeton Battle Monument
description: The monument was designed by the prominent [[Beaux-Arts architecture|Beaux Arts]] sculptor [[Frederick William MacMonnies|Frederick MacMonnies]] with the assistance of architect [[Thomas Hastings (architect)|Thomas Hastings]]. It commemorates the January 3, 1777 [[Battle of Princeton]], and depicts [[George Washington|General George Washington]] leading his troops to victory as well as the death of [[Hugh Mercer|General Hugh Mercer]].  It stands {{convert|50|ft}} tall and was inspired by carvings on the [[Arc de Triomphe]] in [[Paris]].

name: McCormick Hall
image: Princeton University Art Museum Side View.JPG
description: The oldest component of McCormick Hall, home to the [[Princeton University Art Museum]], built 1923 and designed in [[Venetian Gothic]] by [[Ralph Adams Cram]], demolished in 2021 to make way for a new art museum building.

name: Cloister Inn
description: The 16th [[eating clubs at Princeton University|eating club]] to be founded at [[Princeton University]]

name: Princeton University Chapel
description: Built at a cost of $2,000,000 after the previous Marquand Chapel was destroyed by fire in 1920.  Seats nearly 2,000 and was the second largest university chapel in the world when built, after that of [[King's College Chapel, Cambridge|King's College]], Cambridge.<ref>{{cite web|title=History of the Chapel|url=https://www.princeton.edu/religiouslife/chapel/history/|website=Office of Religious Life|publisher=Princeton University}}</ref>

name: Palmer Square Post Office
description: Built during the [[New Deal]], the post office is known for its mural, ''Columbia under the Palm'', painted by Karl Free for the [[Section of Painting and Sculpture]].  The mural has come under criticism for its depiction of the triumph of European settlers over indigenous peoples.<ref>{{cite web|title=Palmer Square Post Office Mural|url=http://livingnewdeal.org/projects/palmer-square-post-office-mural-princeton-nj/|website=The Living New Deal}}</ref>

name: Nassau Inn
description: Princeton's only full-service hotel, dates to 1769, current building to 1938 as part of [[Palmer Square]], Yankee Doodle Tap Room home to [[Norman Rockwell]] mural<ref>{{cite web|title=Our History|url=http://www.nassauinn.com/historic-princeton-hotel/history-en.html|website=Nassau Inn}}</ref>

name: Dillon Gymnasium
description: Replaced University Gymnasium, which burned to the ground in 1944.  Houses a 1,500-seat gymnasium, squash courts and a pool.  Designed by [[Aymar Embury]] and named for Herbert L. Dillon, class of 1907, a one-time football captain.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Leitch|first1=Alexander|title=A Princeton Companion|date=1978|publisher=Princeton University Press|page=137|url=http://etcweb.princeton.edu/CampusWWW/Companion/dillon_gymnasium.html}}</ref>

name: Firestone Library
description: The main library system of [[Princeton University]], named after tire [[magnate]] [[Harvey Firestone]], with holdings of more than 7 million books, 6 million microforms, and 48,000 linear feet of manuscripts<ref>{{cite web|title=Princeton University Library|url=https://www.princeton.edu/main/library/|website=Princeton University}}</ref>
